planting.note: Plant on a sturdy trellis in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun, siting a male Actinidia arguta vine nearby since Ananasnaja is a female cultivar and will not set fruit alone.

directions: Ananasnaja (sometimes sold as Ananasnaya) is a heavy-bearing Russian-bred hardy kiwiberry selection valued for grape-sized, smooth-skinned fruit with a distinctive pineapple-tinged sweetness. Vines are extremely vigorous twining climbers that require a strong permanent trellis or arbor and yearly winter pruning to control growth and encourage fruiting wood renewal. As a female clone it must be planted within about 30 to 50 feet of a compatible male arguta vine for pollination and fruit set. Fruit ripens in early to mid fall and is typically harvested by taste-testing a few berries, since the smooth green skin gives little visual ripeness cue.

planting.note: Plant in spring on a strong trellis in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; Weiki is self-fertile and can be grown as a single vine without a separate male pollinator.

directions: Weiki is a German-bred self-fertile hardy kiwiberry, prized alongside Issai as one of the few Actinidia arguta selections that reliably fruits from a single vine, though yields improve when a male vine is nearby. Fruit is small, smooth-skinned, and sweet with a mild kiwi flavor, ripening in early fall slightly ahead of many standard dioecious cultivars. Vines are vigorous twining climbers needing a permanent trellis or pergola and hard annual pruning to manage growth and keep fruiting spurs productive. Weiki tends to begin bearing at a younger age than many hardy kiwi selections, making it a practical choice where trellis space is limited.

planting.note: Plant a male pollinator vine within 30 to 50 feet, then train the female Michigan State vine onto a strong trellis in full sun and well-drained soil.

directions: Michigan State is a female hardy kiwiberry selection developed at Michigan State University and grown for its exceptional cold hardiness, tolerating winter lows that damage many other Actinidia arguta cultivars. Fruit is grape-sized with smooth green skin and sweet flesh, ripening in early to mid fall. Being dioecious, it requires a separate male arguta vine nearby for pollination and fruit set. Provide a heavy-duty trellis and prune each winter to remove old wood and maintain an open, productive canopy.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in full sun on well-drained soil, staking young trees until established.

directions: Karp's Sweet is a cold-hardy quince selection notable for fruit mild enough to eat fresh out of hand, unlike most quince cultivars that require cooking to be palatable. Trees are compact, self-fertile, and produce fragrant, pear-shaped golden fruit in fall after a single showy spring bloom. Its hardiness makes it a good choice for northern growers where standard Smyrna-type quinces struggle with winter dieback. Site in full sun with good air circulation to reduce fire blight and leaf spot pressure, and thin fruit if branches appear overloaded.

common_name: Elegant Cornelian Cherry (Large-Fruited Cornus mas Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in full sun to part shade on well-drained soil; a second seedling or cultivar nearby improves fruit set.

directions: Elegant is a named cornelian cherry cultivar selected for larger, glossy red fruit than typical seedling Cornus mas, with a tart cherry-like flavor suited to preserves and syrups once fully ripe and slightly soft. Trees bloom on bare branches in very early spring with small yellow flowers that are among the first nectar sources for pollinators after winter. Fruit set improves with a genetically distinct second tree nearby, since seedling-grown Cornus mas is only partially self-fertile. The species is tough and adaptable, tolerating urban conditions, drought once established, and a range of soil types.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in full sun on well-drained, even sandy or poor soil, with a compatible male pollinator planted nearby.

directions: Titan is a Russian-bred female sea buckthorn selection known for unusually large, orange-red berries produced in dense clusters along the branches, borne on thornier growth than some newer German cultivars. As a dioecious shrub it needs a male Hippophae rhamnoides plant within about 50 to 100 feet for pollination and reliable fruit set. Its nitrogen-fixing roots let it thrive in poor, sandy, or gravelly soils where few other fruiting shrubs succeed, and established plants tolerate drought and coastal wind well. Harvest by cutting whole fruiting branches and freezing them, since the tart berries cling tightly to the stem and are difficult to pick by hand when ripe.

common_name: Squibnocket Beach Plum (Named Cape Cod Beach Plum Selection)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun on well-drained, sandy soil, including seaside sites, with a genetically distinct beach plum nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Squibnocket is a named beach plum selection identified from wild coastal populations for its reliable cropping and better-than-average fruit size, part of a group of named clones evaluated for improving on typical unselected seedling beach plum. Shrubs produce abundant white blossom in mid-spring followed by tart-to-sweet purple-red plums in late summer, prized for jams and jellies. Beach plum is naturally adapted to sandy, salt-sprayed, wind-exposed coastal soils and needs excellent drainage rather than rich garden soil to thrive. Because most beach plum is only partially self-fertile, planting more than one genetically distinct shrub greatly improves fruit set.
sources: USDA NRCS Cape May Plant Materials Center

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in full sun to part shade on well-drained soil, staking young trees until they establish.

directions: Royal is a traditional English medlar cultivar grown for centuries for its russet-brown, apple-shaped fruit that must be bletted, or softened by frost and storage, before eating, developing a soft, spiced, wine-like flavor. Trees are small, gnarled, and self-fertile, producing single white blossoms in late spring followed by fruit that ripens hard on the tree into autumn. Harvest fruit after the first hard frost and store in a cool, dark spot for two to three weeks until the flesh softens and darkens before use in preserves or eaten fresh. The species tolerates a range of soils and needs little pruning beyond removing crossing or damaged branches.
